summary:
Meena noticed that when she looked into a curved mirror, her face appeared unusually large, while her brother stood a little farther away and looked upside down. She remembered doing activities with a mirror earlier where the image formed by the mirror was of the same size as the object and was erect. This is because mirrors work on the principle of reflection, where light bounces back from a surface and forms an image that appears to be the same size as the original object.

When Meena stepped closer to one of the curved mirrors, she saw her face appear larger than usual. She also noticed that when she looked into another mirror, she saw a tiny version of herself. This is because mirrors work on the principle of reflection, where light bounces back from a surface and forms an image that appears to be smaller than the original object.

Meena's curiosity grew as she realized that there were different types of mirrors, each with its own unique properties. She remembered learning about concave and convex mirrors in her science class. Concave mirrors are curved inward, while convex mirrors are curved outward. When light falls on a concave mirror, it forms an image that appears larger than the object and is erect.

Meena's teacher explained to her that the size of the image changes as the distance of the object from the mirror changes. This is because mirrors work on the principle of reflection, where light bounces back from a surface and forms an image that appears to be different sizes depending on the distance of the object. Meena was fascinated by this concept and asked her teacher to explain it further. Her teacher showed her how to use a concave mirror as a side-view mirror, road safety mirror, or surveillance mirror, demonstrating its unique properties.

Meena's experiment with convex mirrors also revealed their unique properties. When light falls on a convex mirror, it forms an image that appears smaller than the object and is inverted. Meena was amazed by this property of convex mirrors and asked her teacher to explain why they always form an erect image of the traffic behind. Her teacher explained that convex mirrors are curved outward, which provides a wider area of view for drivers and prevents collisions.

Meena's experiment with plane mirrors also revealed their unique properties. When light falls on a plane mirror, it forms an image that appears the same size as the object and is erect. Meena was amazed by this property of plane mirrors and asked her teacher to explain why they always form an erect image of the traffic behind. Her teacher explained that plane mirrors work on the principle of reflection, where light bounces back from a surface and forms an image that appears to be the same size as the original object.
